      <content name="title"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cutaneous <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">SLE</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Subacute Cutaneous <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Systemic</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span> <span class="qt2">Erythematosus</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Discoid <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>?<p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span> is a chronic (long-lasting) type of autoimmune disease. Autoimmune diseases happen when your immune system attacks healthy cells and tissues by mistake. This attack causes inflammation. It can also damage many parts of the body, including the joints, skin, kidneys, heart, lungs, and brain.</p><p>There are several types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Systemic</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> <span class="qt2">erythematosus</span> (SLE) is the most common type. It can be mild or severe and can affect many parts of the body.</li><li>Cutaneous <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> affects the skin. It causes a rash or sores, usually after your skin is exposed to sunlight. The two major types of cutaneous <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> are discoid <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> and subacute cutaneous <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>.</li><li>Drug-induced <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> is caused by a reaction to some medicines. The symptoms may start 3 to 6 months after starting the medicine. The symptoms usually go away when you stop taking the medicine.</li><li>Neonatal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>, which is rare, affects newborns. It is caused by certain antibodies that are passed from the pregnant mother to the fetus.</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>?<p>The cause of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> is unknown. Researchers are studying what might cause or trigger the disease, such as:</p><ul><li>Genetics</li><li>Environmental factors, such as viral infections, sunlight, certain medicines, and smoking</li><li>Problems with the immune system</li></ul>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>, but women get it much more often than men.</p><p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span> is more common in African Americans than in White people. It is also more common in people of American Indian and Asian descent.  African American and Hispanic women are more likely to have severe forms of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>?<p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span> can have many symptoms, and they differ from person to person. Some of the more common ones are:</p><ul><li>Arthritis, causing painful and swollen joints and morning stiffness</li><li>Fever</li><li>Fatigue or feeling tired often</li><li>Red rash, most often on the face (also called the "butterfly rash")</li><li>Chest pain when taking a deep breath</li><li>Hair loss</li><li>Pale or purple fingers or toes, from cold and stress (Raynaud phenomenon) </li><li>Sensitivity to the sun</li><li>Swelling in legs or around eyes</li><li>Mouth ulcers</li><li>Swollen glands</li><li>Headache and dizziness</li><li>Confusion and memory problems</li></ul><p>Symptoms may come and go. When you are having symptoms, it is called a flare.  Flares can range from mild to severe. New symptoms may appear at any time.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> cause?<p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span> causes inflammation throughout your body. This can cause problems in your organs, including:</p><ul><li>Kidney damage (<span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> nephritis).</li><li>Heart problems, including inflammation in the heart (myocarditis), heart valves, or lining of the heart muscle (pericarditis).</li><li>Inflammation of blood vessels (vasculitis).</li><li>Blood clots</li><li>Inflammation of the tissue that surrounds the lungs (pleurisy). This can make it painful to breathe.</li></ul><p>Some people with <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> may be more likely to develop other conditions, such as coronary artery disease (CAD) and atherosclerosis.</p>How is <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>, and it's often mistaken for other diseases that cause similar symptoms. So it may take a while to get a diagnosis. To find out if you have <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>, your health care provider: </p><ul><li>Will ask about your symptoms, medical history, and family health history</li><li>Will do a complete physical exam</li><li>May order blood tests, such as ANA (antinuclear antibody), antibodies, complete blood count, and complement  tests</li><li>May order other tests, such as urine tests</li><li>May do biopsies:
  <ul><li>Skin biopsy (looking at skin samples under a microscope)</li><li>Kidney biopsy (looking at tissue from your kidney under a microscope)</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>?<p>There is no cure for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>, but medicines and lifestyle changes can help control it.</p><p>People with <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> often need to see different providers. You will most likely have a primary care provider and a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in autoimmune and other diseases of the bones, joints, and muscles). Which other specialists you may need depend on how <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> affects your body. For example, if <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> is damaging your heart or blood vessels, you would see a cardiologist (a doctor who specializes in heart diseases).</p><p>Your primary care provider should coordinate care between all of your other providers and treat other problems as they come up. You and your primary care provider will develop a treatment plan to fit your needs. You will both review the plan often to make sure that it is working. You should report new symptoms to your provider right away so that your treatment plan can be changed, if needed.</p><p></p><p>The goals of a treatment plan are to:</p><ul><li>Prevent flares</li><li>Treat flares when they occur</li><li>Reduce organ damage and other problems</li><li>Improve your quality of life</li></ul><p>Treatments may include drugs to:</p><ul><li>Reduce fever, swelling, and pain</li><li>Reduce inflammation in your body</li><li>Prevent or reduce flares</li><li>Reduce or prevent damage to joints</li><li>Suppress (lower) the activity of your immune system</li></ul><p>Newer medicines are now available for some types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>, including <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> that affects the kidneys. These medicines work by targeting specific parts of the immune system. Besides taking medicines for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>, you may need to take medicines for problems that are related to <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or infections.</p><p>Alternative and complementary therapies are therapies that are not part of standard treatments. Some people try alternative and complementary therapies to improve their <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> symptoms. But research has not clearly shown whether these treatments may help or treat <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>. Talk to your provider before trying any new treatments.</p><p>Researchers are also studying treatments, such as CAR-T cell therapy, for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> that hasn't improved with other medicines. New treatments like this are usually only available by joining a research study, until they're approved for general use.</p>How can I cope with <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>?<p>It is important to take an active role in your treatment. It helps to learn more about <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> - being able to spot the warning signs of a flare can help you prevent the flare or make the symptoms less severe.</p><p>It is also important to find ways to cope with the stress of having <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>. Exercising and finding ways to relax may make it easier for you to cope. A good support system can also help.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title">Joint Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Arthrography</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Arthroplasty</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Arthroscopy</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are joints?<p>Your joints are places where two or more bones come together. Your shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, and knuckles are all joints. Your spine has joints, too.</p><p>But joints are more than bones. They include the soft tissues around them, such as cartilage, tendons and ligaments. Cartilage is the hard slippery flexible tissue that covers the ends of your bones at a joint. Tendons are tough, flexible bands that connect your muscles to your bones so you can move your joints. Ligaments connect the bones of the joint to each other to keep them stable when you move.</p>What are joint disorders?<p>Joint disorders are diseases or injuries that affect your joints. Injuries can happen because of overuse of a joint. Or you could have a sudden injury, such as an accident or a sports injury.</p>What diseases can affect the joints?<p>Many diseases can affect the joints. They often cause joint pain and make your joints stiff, red, or swollen. Most of them are chronic. That means they last a long time. Some may never go away completely. Some of the diseases that affect the joints include:</p><ul><li>Arthritis. Arthritis may cause joint pain and swelling. There are many types of this disease. Osteoarthritis is the most common type. Over time, arthritis can cause severe joint damage. It can affect people of all ages. A joint injury when you're young may cause osteoarthritis later in life.</li><li><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Lupus</span></span>. This autoimmune disease affects many parts of the body and can cause joint and muscle pain. Some types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> often cause arthritis.</li><li>Sjögren's Disease. This autoimmune disease affects glands that make moisture in many parts of the body. The main symptoms are dry eyes and mouth, but it often causes joint pain, too.</li></ul><p>Treatments are different depending on the disease. But most treatments include medicines and therapies to relieve pain and other symptoms.</p>What types of joint disorders happen from sudden injuries?<p>Joint disorders from sudden injuries include:</p><ul><li>Sprains and strains. Sprains are stretched or torn ligaments. Acute strains are stretched or torn muscles or tendons that happen from a sudden injury or movement, such as lifting a heavy object.</li><li>Dislocated joints. A joint is dislocated when the bones are pushed or pulled out of position. A joint dislocation is a medical emergency.</li></ul><p>Treatment depends on the type of injury. You can treat many sports injuries at home. But you should call your health care provider if you:</p><ul><li>Have a lot of joint pain, swelling or numbness</li><li>Can't put weight on the joint</li><li>Have pain from an old injury with more swelling, an unstable joint, or a joint that isn't normal in another way</li></ul>What types of joint disorders happen from overuse?<p>Overuse injuries usually damage the soft tissues of the joint. They can happen when you work a joint too hard by doing the same movements over and over. For example, you could get an overuse injury from playing a musical instrument, playing sports, or doing certain jobs, such as carpentry or painting.</p><p>Joint overuse injuries include:</p><ul><li>Bursitis. The bursa is a small fluid-filled sac. It works as a pad between the bones of a joint and the moving parts around it, such as muscles, tendons and skin. With bursitis, the bursa becomes irritated and swollen with extra fluid. Overuse is the most common cause, but injuries, infections and other conditions, such as arthritis, can cause bursitis.</li><li>Tendinitis. This condition happens when you overuse a tendon. It swells and makes the joint painful to move.</li><li>Chronic strain. A strain becomes chronic when your muscles or tendons stretch or tear slowly over time from repeating the same movements.</li></ul><p>The treatments for bursitis, tendinitis, and chronic strain are often the same. They usually include rest, keeping the injured joint higher than your heart, and taking medicine to reduce swelling. Your provider may recommend gentle exercise and other treatment. In some cases, your provider may suggest an injection (a shot) of medicine into the joint. If these do not help, you may need surgery.</p>How can I keep my joints healthy?<p>Getting enough physical activity is one of the most important things you can do to prevent or slow joint disorders. Activity strengthens the muscles around your joints and helps them work better.</p><p>When you play sports, wear the right equipment to protect your joints, such as knee pads. If you already have joint problems, ask your provider what type of activities are best for you.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/kidneydiseases.html">
      <content name="title">Kidney Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Nephritis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Renal Diseases</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>You have two kidneys, each about the size of your fist. They are near the middle of your back, just below the rib cage. Inside each kidney there are about a million tiny structures called nephrons. They filter your blood. They remove wastes and extra water, which become urine.  The urine flows through tubes called ureters. It goes to your bladder, which stores the urine until you go to the bathroom.</p><p>Most kidney diseases attack the nephrons. This damage may leave kidneys unable to remove wastes. Causes can include genetic problems, injuries, or medicines. You have a higher risk of kidney disease if you have diabetes, high blood pressure, or a close family member with kidney disease. Chronic kidney disease damages the nephrons slowly over several years. Other kidney problems include:</p><ul><li>Cancer</li><li>Cysts</li><li>Stones</li><li>Infections</li></ul><p>Your doctor can do blood and urine tests to check if you have kidney disease. If your kidneys fail, you will need dialysis or a kidney transplant.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/raynaudphenomenon.html">
      <content name="title">Raynaud Phenomenon</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Raynaud's Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Raynaud's Syndrome</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is Raynaud phenomenon? <p>Raynaud phenomenon is a condition that affects your blood vessels (the tubes that your blood flows through). It causes your blood vessels to narrow, which decreases blood flow. This is called a Raynaud episode or "attack." The attacks usually affect your fingers and toes, causing them to become cold and numb. They may also change color, usually to white or blue. These attacks happen in response to cold temperatures or stress.</p><p>Raynaud phenomenon may also be called Raynaud disease or Raynaud syndrome.</p>What are the types of Raynaud phenomenon?<p>There are two types of Raynaud phenomenon:</p><ul><li>Primary Raynaud phenomenon is the more common type. Its cause is unknown.</li><li>Secondary Raynaud phenomenon is usually caused by another disease or problem, such as <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span> or scleroderma. Other causes may be exposure to cold or certain chemicals. This type can be more serious than the primary type.</li></ul>What causes Raynaud phenomenon?<p>Researchers don't know exactly why some people develop Raynaud phenomenon. But they do understand how the attacks happen. When you are exposed to cold, your body tries to slow the loss of heat and maintain its temperature. To do this, the blood vessels in the top layer of your skin constrict (narrow). This moves blood from those vessels near the surface to vessels deeper in the body. But when you have Raynaud phenomenon, the blood vessels in your hands and feet react to cold or stress by narrowing quickly. They also stay narrowed for a long time.</p>Who is more likely to develop Raynaud phenomenon? <p>Anyone can develop Raynaud phenomenon, but some people are more likely to develop it:</p><ul><li>Primary Raynaud phenomenon has been linked to:
  <ul><li>Your sex. Women get it more often than men.</li><li>Your age. It usually develops in people younger than age 30. It often starts in the teenage years.</li><li>A family history of Raynaud phenomenon. You are more likely to develop Raynaud phenomenon if you have a family member who has it.</li></ul>
</li><li>Secondary Raynaud phenomenon has been linked to:
  <ul><li>Certain diseases. These include <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), carpal tunnel syndrome, and connective tissue disorders.</li><li>Certain medicines. Medicines that treat high blood pressure, migraines, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may cause similar symptoms to Raynaud phenomenon or make your symptoms worse.</li><li>Work-related exposures, such as repeated use of vibrating machinery (such as a jackhammer), or exposure to cold or certain chemicals.</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the symptoms of Raynaud phenomenon?<p>Raynaud attacks most often happen when you get cold, for example when you grab something cold from the freezer or go into an air-conditioned building on a warm day. Attacks usually affect your fingers and toes. But sometimes they can affect other parts of your body, such as your ears, nose, lips, or nipples.</p><p>An attack causes the skin to become cold and numb. Your skin may also turn white or blue due to a lack of oxygen. As the blood flow returns, your skin may tingle, throb, or turn red. An attack may last a few minutes or a few hours. If you have darker skin, you may not be able to easily see the skin color changes.</p><p>For many people, especially those with the primary type, the symptoms are mild. People with the secondary type often have more severe symptoms. They may develop skin ulcers (open sores caused by poor blood flow) or skin infections.</p>How is Raynaud phenomenon diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test to diagnose Raynaud phenomenon. To find out if you have it, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will take your medical history and ask about your symptoms.</li><li>Will do a physical exam.</li><li>May order blood and other lab tests to check for other conditions which could be causing your symptoms and/or to help decide which type of Raynaud phenomenon you have.</li></ul>What are the treatments for Raynaud phenomenon?<p>Most people with Raynaud phenomenon can keep their symptoms under control by avoiding getting cold. But if this is not enough, medicines and, in some cases, surgical procedures can help.</p><p>Secondary Raynaud phenomenon is more likely to be serious and to need more treatments. It's also important to treat the condition or problem that is causing your Raynaud phenomenon. </p><p>You may need to see a specialist such as a rheumatologist, a doctor who treats diseases of the joints, muscles, and bones.</p>Can Raynaud phenomenon be prevented?<p>Raynaud phenomenon cannot be prevented, but you can help prevent attacks and manage your symptoms by:</p><ul><li>Placing your hands or feet in a warm place when you have an attack. This could mean putting them under warm (not hot) water or under a heating pad.</li><li>Keeping your body, especially your hands and feet, warm in cold weather.</li><li>Avoiding triggers, such as certain medicines and stress.</li><li>Quitting smoking (or not starting smoking).</li><li>Managing stress.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/arthritis.html">
      <content name="title">Arthritis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Joint inflammation</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is arthritis?<p>If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have arthritis. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called arthritis. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee.</p><p>Most types of arthritis can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of arthritis can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of arthritis you have.</p>What are the types of arthritis?<p>Common types of arthritis include:</p><ul><li>Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It's often related to aging or injury.</li><li>Autoimmune arthritis happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake.  Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of this type of arthritis.</li><li>Juvenile arthritis is a type of arthritis that happens in children.</li><li>Infectious arthritis is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive arthritis is one type.</li><li>Psoriatic arthritis affects people with psoriasis (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches).</li><li>Gout is a painful type of arthritis that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected.</li><li>Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of arthritis?<p>Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common arthritis symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever, weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash.</p><p>Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of arthritis may be signs of other illnesses.</p>Who is more likely to get arthritis?<p>A few things that might increase your chance of getting arthritis include:</p><ul><li>Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of arthritis if a member of your family has the disorder.</li><li>Age. The risk of getting many types of arthritis increases with age.</li><li>Sex. Certain types of arthritis are more common in women, while other types are more common in men.</li></ul><p>Other factors that might increase your risk of getting arthritis include having a previous joint injury, obesity, or <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">lupus</span></span>.</p>How is arthritis diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have arthritis, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask you about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or take x-rays.</li></ul><p>Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in arthritis care) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for arthritis?<p>Treatment depends on the type of arthritis you have. It may include medicine or surgery. Your provider will work with you to improve your symptoms and quality of life.</p><p>A few ways to help manage your symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Hot or cold packs</li><li>Relaxation techniques</li><li>Use of splints, braces, and/or assistive devices</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>
